claims.text: An interatomic machine-learning potential can be trained on ab initio solid and liquid configurations of multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting points.
Such a machine-learning potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap relative to traditional EAM references used in TOR-TILD.
Improved phase-space overlap will significantly reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The training data should include both solid and liquid configurations and capture the diversity of atomic configurations in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed intervention applies to multicomponent high-entropy alloys with three or more principal elements.
The intervention is applicable to both solid and liquid states near the alloys' melting temperatures.
Machine-learning potentials inherently include many-body interactions.
A machine-learning potential can accurately represent the diverse local atomic environments present in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Representing diverse atomic environments more accurately will bring the reference and ab initio configuration spaces closer together.
Fixed-form EAM potentials miss features of the complex energy landscape and local atomic interactions in high-entropy alloys.
Data-driven adaptation to the energy landscape will produce better phase-space overlap and a shorter, less mismatched thermodynamic-integration path.
The machine-learning reference may reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
Reducing path mismatch will lead to more accurate free-energy calculations.
TOR-TILD EAM references suffer from significant phase-space-overlap problems for ab initio liquid high-entropy alloys.
Poor phase-space overlap with TOR-TILD EAM references produces larger thermodynamic-integration path mismatches.
The benefits of the intervention may not extend to elemental or binary systems or to conditions far from melting.
Performance depends on training-data quality and coverage and on transferability across compositions and temperatures.
Failure to reduce path mismatch by at least approximately 30% relative to EAM, or failure to move the calculated free energy closer to an ab initio benchmark, would falsify the hypothesis.
